items.name: The Big Bang
facts: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago as a hot, dense point and has been expanding ever since.
Space itself expanded; the Big Bang was not an explosion into empty space.
In its first few minutes the universe made the nuclei of hydrogen and helium.

items.name: Cosmic inflation
facts: In a tiny fraction of a second, the universe grew enormously in size.
Inflation explains why the universe looks so smooth and even in every direction.
Tiny ripples from this time later grew into galaxies.

items.name: First atoms and the cosmic microwave background
facts: After about 380,000 years, the universe cooled enough for electrons to join nuclei and form atoms.
Light could then travel freely for the first time.
That ancient light is still all around us today as the cosmic microwave background.
It was discovered by accident in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson.

items.name: The cosmic dark ages
facts: After the first atoms formed there were no stars, so the universe was dark.
Gas slowly clumped together under gravity.
This period lasted more than 100 million years.

items.name: The first stars
facts: The first stars lit up roughly 100 to 200 million years after the Big Bang.
They were huge, hot and short-lived, made only of hydrogen and helium.
Their light helped burn away the fog of neutral gas, ending the dark ages.

items.name: The first galaxies
facts: Gravity pulled stars and gas together into the first small galaxies.
The James Webb Space Telescope has seen galaxies from about 300 million years after the Big Bang.
Small galaxies merged over time to build bigger ones.

items.name: Heavy elements from supernovae
facts: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium, then into heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen.
When a big star dies in a supernova, it scatters these elements into space.
The carbon in your body and the iron in your blood were made inside stars.

items.name: The Milky Way forms
facts: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, began forming within about a billion years of the Big Bang.
It grew by swallowing smaller galaxies.
Today it holds 100 to 400 billion stars and is about 100,000 light years across.

items.name: Dark energy speeds up expansion
facts: About 5 to 6 billion years ago the expansion of the universe began to speed up.
The cause is called dark energy; nobody knows what it is.
Astronomers found this in 1998 by studying distant exploding stars.

items.name: The Sun forms
facts: A cloud of gas and dust collapsed under gravity, and the Sun lit up at its centre.
The leftover disc of dust and gas formed the planets.
The Sun holds 99.8 per cent of the mass of the Solar System.

items.name: Earth forms
facts: Dust and rocks in the disc stuck together to build the Earth.
Earth's age of 4.54 billion years comes from dating meteorites and the oldest rocks.
The young Earth was hot, molten and had no oceans.

items.name: The Moon-forming impact
facts: A Mars-sized body, often called Theia, crashed into the young Earth.
Debris thrown into orbit came together to form the Moon.
Moon rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts support this idea.

items.name: Oceans form
facts: Earth cooled and water vapour condensed to make the first oceans.
Tiny zircon crystals from Australia suggest liquid water by about 4.4 billion years ago.
Some of the water may have arrived on comets and asteroids.

items.name: Late Heavy Bombardment
facts: Many large asteroids and comets struck the Earth and Moon.
Many of the big craters on the Moon may date from this time.
Scientists still argue about whether it was one burst or a slow decline.

items.name: First life
facts: Simple single-celled microbes appeared in the oceans.
The oldest likely fossils are stromatolites, mounds built by microbes, about 3.5 billion years old.
Possible traces of life in Greenland rocks are about 3.7 billion years old.

items.name: Photosynthesis begins
facts: Some microbes learned to use sunlight to make food.
Early photosynthesis did not make oxygen.
Later, cyanobacteria began to release oxygen as waste, some time before 2.4 billion years ago.

items.name: Great Oxidation Event
facts: Oxygen from cyanobacteria built up in the air for the first time.
It killed many microbes that could not cope with oxygen.
Iron in the oceans rusted, leaving red bands in rocks we can see today.

items.name: First eukaryotes
facts: Cells with a nucleus appeared; these are called eukaryotes.
They formed when one cell took in another, which became the mitochondria.
All plants, animals and fungi are made of eukaryotic cells.

items.name: Multicellular life
facts: Cells began living together as single organisms.
A red alga called Bangiomorpha, about 1 billion years old, is one of the earliest known examples.
Multicellular life evolved separately many times.

items.name: Cambrian explosion
facts: Most major animal groups appeared within a few tens of millions of years.
Animals grew hard shells, eyes and legs, and began to hunt each other.
The Burgess Shale in Canada preserves strange soft-bodied animals from this time.

items.name: First land plants
facts: Small moss-like plants began to grow on land.
Their spores are found in rocks about 470 million years old.
Plants on land changed the soil and the air.

items.name: First land animals
facts: Small arthropods such as millipedes were among the first animals to live on land.
One of the oldest known, found in Scotland, is over 400 million years old.
Land animals needed ways to breathe air and stop drying out.

items.name: First insects
facts: The oldest known insect fossil, from Scotland, is about 400 million years old.
Insects were the first animals to fly, by about 325 million years ago.
Today insects make up more than half of all known species.

items.name: First forests
facts: Tall trees appeared and formed the first forests.
The oldest known forest fossils are in New York State, about 385 million years old.
Forests pulled carbon dioxide from the air and cooled the planet.

items.name: First reptiles
facts: Reptiles were the first animals to lay eggs with a shell, so they could breed away from water.
One of the oldest, Hylonomus, was found inside fossil tree stumps in Nova Scotia.
At this time much of the land was covered in swampy coal forests.

items.name: Permian extinction
facts: The biggest mass extinction ever killed most species in the sea, perhaps 80 to 90 per cent.
Huge volcanic eruptions in Siberia are the likely cause.
It is sometimes called the Great Dying.

items.name: First dinosaurs
facts: The earliest dinosaurs were small, and lived in what is now Argentina and Brazil.
Dinosaurs ruled the land for about 165 million years.
All the continents were joined in one landmass, Pangaea.

items.name: First mammals
facts: The first mammals were small, furry and active at night.
They lived alongside the dinosaurs for over 130 million years.
Mammals feed their young on milk and are warm-blooded.

items.name: Flowering plants
facts: Flowering plants appeared in the Cretaceous period.
They spread quickly, helped by insects that carried their pollen.
Today about 9 in 10 plant species have flowers.

items.name: Chicxulub impact
facts: An asteroid about 10 kilometres wide hit what is now Mexico.
Dust and soot blocked the Sun, and plants and food chains collapsed.
All dinosaurs except birds died out, along with about three quarters of all species.
The crater lies half under the sea near the town of Chicxulub.

items.name: First primates
facts: After the dinosaurs died out, mammals spread into new roles.
Early primates were small tree-dwellers with grasping hands and forward-facing eyes.
They were the ancestors of lemurs, monkeys, apes and humans.

items.name: First apes
facts: Apes split from monkeys; apes have no tail and bigger brains.
Humans share about 98 to 99 per cent of their DNA with chimpanzees.
The human and chimp lines separated about 6 to 7 million years ago.

items.name: Australopithecus
facts: These early human relatives walked upright but had small brains.
The famous skeleton Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974, is about 3.2 million years old.
Footprints at Laetoli in Tanzania show upright walking 3.7 million years ago.

items.name: Homo habilis
facts: One of the earliest species in our own group, Homo.
Its name means handy man, because it was found with stone tools.
The oldest known stone tools, from Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, even older than Homo habilis.

items.name: Homo erectus
facts: Homo erectus had a bigger brain and a body shape much like ours.
It was the first human species to spread out of Africa into Asia.
It made teardrop-shaped hand axes.

items.name: Control of fire
facts: Burned bones and ash in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, suggest fire use about 1 million years ago.
Regular use of fire is clear by about 400,000 years ago.
Cooking made food easier to digest and may have helped brains grow.

items.name: Neanderthals
facts: Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia.
They were strong, had big brains, made tools and buried their dead.
They died out about 40,000 years ago, but most people today carry some Neanderthal DNA.

items.name: Homo sapiens
facts: Our own species appeared in Africa.
The oldest known fossils were found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco.
Every person alive today belongs to Homo sapiens.

items.name: Out of Africa
facts: Modern humans spread from Africa into Asia, Europe and Australia.
People reached Australia by about 65,000 years ago and Europe by about 45,000.
Later they crossed into the Americas, by at least 15,000 years ago.

items.name: Cave art
facts: The oldest known cave paintings are in Sulawesi, Indonesia, and show animals and human-like figures.
In Europe, Chauvet Cave in France has paintings about 36,000 years old.
Lascaux in France was painted about 17,000 years ago.

items.name: End of the last Ice Age
facts: The last cold period ended and the warm Holocene epoch began.
Melting ice sheets raised sea levels by more than 100 metres.
Britain became an island about 8,000 years ago when the land bridge to Europe, Doggerland, flooded.

items.name: Farming begins
facts: People in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East began to grow wheat and barley.
They kept sheep, goats, pigs and cattle.
Farming arose separately in China, the Americas, Africa and New Guinea.
Settled farming led to villages, then towns and cities.

items.name: Oceans boil away
facts: The Sun slowly gets brighter, by about 10 per cent every billion years.
In about a billion years Earth will be too hot for liquid water.
Complex life on Earth will probably end long before the Sun dies.

items.name: Milky Way meets Andromeda
facts: The Andromeda galaxy is heading towards us at about 110 kilometres per second.
The two galaxies are expected to merge into one, sometimes called Milkomeda.
Stars are so far apart that almost none will collide.
Some newer studies say a near miss is also possible.

items.name: Sun becomes a red giant
facts: The Sun will run out of hydrogen in its core and swell up into a red giant.
It will swallow Mercury and Venus and may swallow Earth.
Afterwards it will shrink to a white dwarf, a hot ember about the size of Earth.
